paragraphs: In America the passion for physical well-being is not always exclusive, but it is general. Not everyone feels it in the same way, yet everyone feels it. Carefully satisfying every need of the body, even the smallest, and providing the little conveniences of life is the first thing on everyone’s mind. Something similar is more and more visible in Europe. Several of the causes that produce these like results in both hemispheres are so closely tied to my subject that they deserve notice.

When wealth is fixed in families by inheritance, a great many people enjoy the comforts of life without developing an exclusive taste for them. The human heart is not so much captured by calmly possessing something valuable as by the desire to have it, while that desire is still only partly satisfied, and by the unceasing fear of losing it. In aristocratic communities the wealthy have never known any condition other than their own, so they have no fear of changing it; the very idea of such a change hardly occurs to them. For them the comforts of life are not the goal of life but simply a way of living. They regard those comforts as existence itself, something enjoyed but scarcely thought about. The natural, instinctive taste that all men feel for being well off is thus satisfied without effort and without worry, and so their faculties turn elsewhere and attach themselves to harder and loftier undertakings, which stir and absorb their minds. That is why the members of an aristocracy, in the midst of physical gratifications, often show a haughty contempt for those very pleasures and an unusual power to endure being deprived of them. Every revolution that has ever shaken or destroyed an aristocracy has shown how easily men used to superfluous luxuries can do without the necessities of life. Men who have labored to earn a modest competence, by contrast, can hardly go on living once they have lost it.

If I turn my attention from the upper to the lower classes, I find similar effects produced by opposite causes. In a nation where aristocracy dominates society and keeps it from changing, the people in the end become as used to poverty as the rich are to their opulence. The rich give no anxious thought to their physical comforts, because they enjoy them without effort. The poor do not think about things they despair of ever getting and know too little about even to desire. In communities of this kind, the imagination of the poor is driven to seek another world. The miseries of real life hem it in, but it slips out of their grip and flies off to find its pleasures far beyond. When, on the contrary, distinctions of rank are blurred and privileges destroyed, when hereditary property is divided up and education and freedom are widely spread, the desire to acquire the comforts of this world haunts the imagination of the poor, and the fear of losing them haunts the imagination of the rich. Many small fortunes spring up. Those who hold them have enough physical gratification to acquire a taste for these pleasures, but not enough to satisfy it. They never get these pleasures without effort, and they never indulge in them without anxiety. They are therefore always straining to pursue or to hold on to gratifications that are so delightful, so imperfect and so fleeting.

Suppose I ask what passion comes most naturally to men who are both spurred on and hemmed in by humble birth or modest fortune. I could find none more peculiarly suited to their condition than this love of physical prosperity. The passion for physical comforts is essentially a passion of the middle classes. With those classes it grows and spreads, and among them it prevails. From there it rises into the higher ranks of society and descends into the mass of the people. In America I never met a citizen so poor that he did not cast a glance of hope and envy at the pleasures of the rich, or whose imagination did not seize in advance on the good things that fate still stubbornly withheld from him. On the other hand, among the wealthier inhabitants of the United States I never noticed that proud contempt for physical gratifications that is sometimes found even in the richest and most dissolute aristocracies. Most of these wealthy men were once poor. They have felt the sting of want, and they were long at the mercy of adverse fortune. Now that the victory is won, the passions that went with the struggle have outlasted it, and their minds are, as it were, intoxicated by the small enjoyments they have pursued for forty years. It is not that in the United States, as elsewhere, there are no wealthy people who inherited their property and possess, without effort, an opulence they have not earned. But even these men are no less devoted to the pleasures of material life. The love of well-being has now become the dominant taste of the nation. The great current of men’s passions runs in that channel and sweeps everything along with it.
